1906.heavy: 'a non-(C)V (i.e. heavy) syllable' vs light '(C)V' (p. 18): any syllable that is not (C)V. The one printed stress example is a closed syllable (/wempakane/ -> [wém.pa.ká:.ne]; syllable codas are a nasal or a glottal, /h/ in Tiriyó, /ʔ/ in Akuriyó, p. 18; 'vowel length does not occur in closed syllables'); the chapter also gives phonemic long vowels ('Long vowels occur phonemically in Tiriyó, and apparently also in Akuriyó', p. 16) and diphthongs with /i, u/ as second element in all three languages (p. 17; /əo/ only in Akuriyó), which are non-(C)V by the same definition, though no CVV stress example is printed.
1906.dflt: Left-to-right iambic alternation: 2nd, 4th, 6th... syllables stressed, never the final one (Tiriyó examples [a.má:.ta.ká:.na], [kɨ.tá:.po.tó:.ma.pó:.ti], [si.rí:.ri.me]; Akuriyó said to be similar). Implied light-syllable grids: 3 syll 010, 4 syll 0100, 5 syll 01010, 7 syll 0101010; nothing stated for 2-, 6- or 8-syllable words or for what happens when the beat would fall on the final syllable.
1906.prule: Iambic rhythmic stress counted from the left edge: in words made of light (C)V syllables every second syllable (2nd, 4th...) is stressed and the final syllable is never stressed; a heavy (non-(C)V: the printed example is a closed syllable; long vowels and diphthongs are also non-(C)V by the source's definition) syllable is obligatorily stressed and the alternation restarts after it. The rule is stated in full for Tiriyó and extended to Akuriyó with hedges ('Akuriyó appears to have a similar system'; the glottal stop 'seems to be part of the rhythmic stress system'). In Akuriyó the stress correlate is glottalization (syllable-final glottal stop), often replacing and sometimes co-occurring with vowel length. No single culminative primary-stress syllable is singled out.
1906.srule: Rhythmic ('secondary', fn. 2) stresses: every second light (C)V syllable counting from the left edge and every heavy (closed) syllable, the count restarting after a heavy syllable; never the word-final syllable. Akuriyó correlate: an automatic syllable-final glottal stop 'corresponding to vowel lengthening in Tiriyó'. Stated for Tiriyó and extended to Akuriyó tentatively ('appears to have a similar system'); the source singles out none of these beats as primary.

Crass 2005 (first-hand, K'abeena) calls the same architecture 'stress accent' (excerpt p.30 cites the HEC 'stress accent languages' classification and Appleyard's tonal-to-stress development). Mous 2021 p.4 (second-hand) lists both varieties among Cushitic 'stress languages'. Tadesse Girma 2024 (K'abeena) found no lexical or grammatical tone and says the language 'doesn't look a pitch-accent language, but further research is needed'. The phonetic label (pitch vs stress) differs between describers; the placement facts do not.

1910.dq: The phonological word is composed of a stem (two or three syllables) and its prefixes, suffixes and enclitics. It is defined as a sequence of syllables which can be spoken in isolation and which has only one stress.
1910.prule: One stress per phonological word (stem + prefixes + suffixes + enclitics, 1-7 syllables), anchored to the stem, not to the word edge: on the initial syllable of the disyllabic couplet (= stem penult) and on the penultimate syllable of a trisyllabic stem; prefixes and enclitics are outside the count (in the 7-syllable šìnàsa'náʔaràñá the stress sits on syllable 4, i.e. 4th from the right edge); the 1sg postclitic -ì shifts stress to the stem-final syllable (Rule 9). Monosyllabic particles (či, nda, ta) are normally unstressed proclitics but carry their own stress as a separate phonological word before a maximal 7-syllable word.

1912.prule: Stress falls on the root (stem) vowel when the stem form contains one (light/heavy/full stems), otherwise on a suffix vowel (short, vowelless stem); the inchoative /Vy/ and transitive irrealis /V?V/ suffixes are nearly always stressed. Explicitly not sensitive to weight or syllable structure.

1914.tone: Three phonemic level tones H, M, L (5.1-5.3; phonemic status of M argued in 5.3); contour tones (falling, rising) are derived, not underlying, arising from floating tones left by vowel deletion (4.1.1) or devocalisation to glides (4.1.4); tone patterns given by syllable count for mono- to quadrisyllabic words (5.4); tonal processes: tone docking, tone fusion, regressive tone spreading, Meeussen's rule (5.5). tn.quote: Ambele is a tone language. That is one which uses tones to distinguish meaning. According to Pike (1945), a tone language is that which has lexically significant, contrastive but relative pitch on each syllable. … The Ambele language has three phonemic tones: the high, mid and low tones (H, M.L). Contour tones in this language are derived from floating tones docking onto the adjacent fone bearing unit (TBU). These floating tones result from vowel deletion (4.1.1) or from vowels which devocalise into glides (4.1.4).

evidence_works.detail: p.206: 'In most Quechua dialects stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel of each polysyllabic word form... Exceptionally, in interjections and emphatic expressions, stress can be word-final, e.g. in alaláw ‘how cold!’.' and 'In the Quechua I dialects stress is maintained in word-final position when the long vowel morpheme referring to first-person subject or possessor is immediately followed by a word boundary. (Length oppositions not connected with the first-person morpheme are normally neutralised in word-final position, in which case stress is regularly assigned to the penultimate syllable.)' p.185 places 'the Andean sector of the department of Pasco' in the Yaru subgroup (c) of Quechua I. Adds: the entry's penultimate rule plus final-stressed first-person long vowel is the general Quechua I pattern and so applies to the Yaru group that holds Ambo-Pasco; a family-wide note that interjections and emphatic expressions can carry final stress; final length outside the first-person marker is neutralised, so penultimate stress is regular there. The weight-dependent deviants named on p.207 are 'QI Ancash and QI Cajatambo' (Torero 1964; Parker 1976), not Pasco; the source does not say that the Yaru group as a whole is weight-insensitive (p.185 puts parts of the province of Cajatambo inside Yaru).

1916.dq: Stress tends to occur on the second last syllable of the word. ... Word stress tends to be lost to phrase stress which is often accompanied by length and often falls on the last syllable of the word in focus.
1916.dloc: sec. 5.3.1 'Phonemic Status of Stress and Length', p.31. OPD: p.4. Laycock: pp.29-30 (sec. 5.21-5.24.3); Laycock stress examples checked on p.30 (accents are lost in).
1916.heavy: Vowel quality tied to intrinsic length: a penult with /ɨ/ (high central, 'the shortest in length') repels stress to the antepenult in 3-5-syllable words (in trisyllables also penult /i/ or /u/); /aa/ (low central, 'the longest') in the last syllable of disyllabic verbs always takes the stress.
1916.prule: General rule: stress on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word (P. Wilson's 1977 supplement, replacing the 1970 stress pages), conditioned on the vowel: a penult with /ɨ/ sends stress to the antepenult in 3-5-syllable words (in trisyllables also penult /i/ or /u/, or V1 aa/e + V2 a); disyllabic verbs with /aa/ in the last syllable stress it; disyllables may have even stress; suffix classes fix antepenult (-ran, -ɨte, -ute, -katik) or final (-k, -n, -u, -o) stress. Hedged ('usually', 'tends to'); non-contrastive.
1916.srule: Stated in the cited work: 1977 suppl. p.14 'If the word contains more than five syllables a secondary stress falls on the fourth or fifth last syllable'; p.15 endings -u, -o: 'stress on final syllable and light stress on third or fourth last syllable'; superseded 1970 p.31: in four-syllable words 'there may be light stress on both the first and third syllables'. Position disjunctive, so not encoded in the rule string.

1917.prule: No rule of record: reachable first-hand sources are irreconcilable. Mullen 1986 (p. 164) states a regular weight-sensitive rule: word-final consonant extrametrical, all other codas heavy; stress the rightmost non-final heavy syllable (heavy final only in disyllables with a light first syllable), else the leftmost syllable. Hayward & Hayward 1992 (p. 51) state that stress is weak and its position variable. Kellogg & Barnes 2026 (16 Addis Ababa speakers, focus-controlled carriers, reported in Kellogg & Bayu 2026) find no acoustic word-level stress at any predicted position, only Accentual-Phrase initial strengthening and a final H boundary tone; Kellogg & Bayu 2026 (stress-'deafness' perception test) conclude the data favour a non-stress account. Leslau 1995 (pp. 44-45) gives hedged tendencies only: near-even stress, never final, disyllabic nouns initial, quadrisyllabic nouns penult, trisyllables vary, pre-geminate syllable 'likely' stressed, shift before the copula naw.

conflict.would_settle: A third live position (Kaech 2022: quantity-insensitive stem-penult/antepenult by category, one speaker) makes this a three-way disagreement, and both instrumental camps exist (Sande et al. 2019 isolated words: intensity correlates of word stress; Kellogg & Barnes focus-controlled carriers: none), so no read work supersedes another. What would settle it: (1) the full production study Kellogg & Barnes in press, 'Word- and phrase-level prosody in Amharic', ACAL 55, Language Science Press (open access when published; bibliography row 22, access 'unknown') — whether its items test Mullen's rightmost-heavy and Kaech's stem-antepenult positions and not only geminate-closed syllables; (2) Alemayehu Haile 1987 'Lexical stress in Amharic', JES 20: 19-43 (bibliography row 20, JSTOR, paywalled) and Wedekind & Wedekind 1994 (row 18, print only), the two dedicated pre-2000 treatments nobody could read; (3) decisively, an instrumental study of the same polysyllabic nouns and verbs in isolation vs in non-final focus-neutral carrier position with several Addis Ababa speakers, testing whether Kaech's single F0 peak per isolated word is a word-level head or an AP boundary phenomenon.

1917.cfw: Mullen 1986 and Sande & Hedding 2014 describe weight-sensitive stress drawn to closed or geminate-closed syllables, Kaech 2022 finds fixed stress on the penult of verb stems and the antepenult of noun stems with no role for weight, Kellogg & Barnes 2026 find no acoustic word stress at all, and Leslau 1995 and Hayward & Hayward 1992 call stress weak, near-even or variable, so both the type of system and the place of stress are under active debate among first-hand studies.

1926.prule: Culminative word prominence realized as a higher pitch ('tono de voz más alto') on one vowel per word, written with an acute on every cited form; the source states no rule for which syllable carries it, and in its own lexicon the marked syllable varies between words of the same shape (amáka 'tree', apáka 'basket', anápa 'macaw' penult vs anaká 'head', araká 'moon', anokwá 'mother' final; tsíma 'doncella fish' vs motó 'agouti'; náakero 'caiman' initial), so placement is lexically specified.

1926.tone: The source describes the prominence only in pitch terms: one part of every word is pronounced 'con un tono de voz más alto', marked with an acute ('tilde'); the only stress-like word is the orthographic 'acentuámos' (where to write the mark on a long vowel). It never calls the language tonal, never uses 'acento'/'stress' analytically, and gives no placement rule. SAPhon's Andoa entry (same Berkeley group, citing Michael, Wauters & Beier in prep.) codes tone: False, so this is a culminative, pitch-realized, lexically placed accent rather than a tone system; lexical is the close alternative reading if 'tono de voz más alto' is taken as a community-primer gloss for stress. Peeke 1954 (2023 reprint, in the copy consulted) only records the impression 'una lengua nasal y de alta tonalidad; que tiene tal vez un ritmo complicado' and explicitly defers phonetics ('la discusión de estos asuntos fonéticos no atañen al presente trabajo'); her example words carry acutes with no statement of what they mark.

tn.quote: Cada palabra del idioma katsakáti tiene una parte que pronunciamos con un tono de voz más alto que las demás partes. Señalamos con una tilde la vocal que se pronuncia con el tono alto: ocháte ¡vamos ya! ... En general, cada palabra tiene un solo tono alto, pero algunas palabras muy largas tienen más de uno. Si los dos tonos son igualmente altos, usamos la misma tilde para los dos. En cambio, si un tono es ligeramente más bajo que el otro, usamos una tilde diferente (`) para ese tono (no tan alto) y una normal (´) para el tono más alto: ijátyawkwáro zúngaro blanco kwajàkeró boa
tn.translation: Every word of Katsakáti has one part that we pronounce with a higher tone of voice than the other parts. We mark with an accent the vowel pronounced with the high tone: ocháte 'let's go now!' ... In general each word has a single high tone, but some very long words have more than one. If the two tones are equally high we use the same accent mark for both. If instead one tone is slightly lower than the other, we use a different mark (`) for that (not so high) tone and a normal one (´) for the higher tone: ijátyawkwáro 'white zúngaro catfish', kwajàkeró 'boa'.

1927.tone: Landaburu 2000 §10.1.1: 'La lengua andoque es tonal'; §10.1.5: two contrastive tonemes (baja/alta) per syllable, surface low/mid/high by six context rules incl. pause-conditioned mid and lowering; lexical minimal pairs (-ka- 'mezclar' vs -ká- 'repartir') and grammatical ones (person indices, real vs virtual mood); 'la tonalidad no diferencia muchos signos'; H tone tends to lengthen the vowel, which the author reads as a possible first step toward dismantling a low-yield tone system. Nothing on stress or accent anywhere in the sketch (a full-text search of the scan's for acent/intensi/promin/stress gives zero hits; the only prominence wording is p. 277 'si... la segunda vocal adquiere relieve prosódico', an incidental remark). Corroboration in the same author's other work: Landaburu 1977 Amerindia 2 'Guide de lecture': 'L'andoke a deux registres. On ne note que le tonème haut' + three sandhi rules, no accent; Landaburu 2004-05 Amerindia 29/30 p. 13 lists andoque among 'lenguas tonales de dos o tres registros' and contrasts these with 'lenguas acento-tonales que guardan oposiciones de registro pero solamente sobre la sílaba resaltada'. Witte 1977 SILPL 52 fn. 1: 'Only high tone is written in the orthography, and that only on syllables other than the penultimate' -- an orthographic convention, not a stress statement. Aikhenvald & Dixon 1999: 371 (second-hand) read Landaburu 1979: 48-51 as three tonal distinctions.

tn.translation: 10.1.5. Tone. Part of the identity of the signifier of an Andoque morpheme is not only the determination of its successive phonemes but also the determination of its successive tonemes. The toneme is the fundamental contrastive melodic pitch of a syllable. There are only two fundamental pitches: one low, one high. ... We call tone the realization of a toneme. In connected speech low, mid and high tones occur. The mid tone is the realization of a low toneme when it stands between a high toneme and a low toneme (rule 1) or between a low toneme and pause (rule 2).

tn.note: Two level tonemes (low, high) on every syllable; surface low/mid/high by six context rules (H after H is low before H or pause). Low yield; H tends to lengthen its vowel. Nothing on stress.

1931.prule: Accent is retracted 'as far as possible' but never beyond the antepenultimate; if the penultimate is long (long vowel or diphthong: the sole example is kaí in dekhalᵃkaínhⁱ, contrasted with antepenult lá in dekhalákainhⁱ) the accent falls on the penult; otherwise on the antepenult. Given as 'the general rule' with unlisted exceptions marked ad hoc by an acute (dekhᵃláhᵘ̃ 'I saw'). The syllable-counting conventions of clause (d) (ai/au = two syllables; final imperfect i/u and silent final a not counted) are stated 'for the above rules' a-c of the Rule of the Short Antepenultimate, which is a separate section under its own heading; they are not part of the accent statement, and the accent example works only if kaí is a single long penult and the final -nhⁱ is the ultima.
1931.quote: As regards Accent, the general rule is to throw it back as far as possible, but there are exceptions, and in such case the accent will be indicated by a ′ on the accented vowel, as in dekhᵃláhᵘ̃ quoted above. 1931.cfw: Angika's stress rests solely on Grierson's 1903 general rule for Maithili and Bihari as a whole (accent as far back as the antepenult, a long penult attracting it), transferred to Angika because he classed the Chhikā-chhikī speech of Bhagalpur as Maithili and declined to describe it separately; nothing written on Angika itself (Chandan Kumar 2019, Suman 2022, Satyam Kumar 2025, Kumari 2025, Preetam Kumar 2026) mentions stress, and for Maithili proper Jha 1958 gives a penultimate default while Yadav 1984 rejects weight-based stress rules outright.
